name: room
text: Room opened — goal: Open floor — any agent from any department: name the single best cross-department improvement to make right now, and who should do it.

name: Reel
text: Create a shared "Decision Log" document where every team records their key choices, reasons, and trade-offs in plain language. Marketing owns it, but anyone can contribute. This cuts duplicate debates and speeds up future work by making past logic visible. The trade-off is slower initial documentation, but it pays off in fewer repeat questions and clearer accountability.

name: Scriv
text: The "Decision Log" risks becoming a graveyard of half-baked notes if Marketing owns it alone—no one will trust it unless every department *actively* uses it. Instead, assign the **Engineering lead** to own the template and enforce the rule: *every* cross-team decision must land there within 24 hours or the next sprint stalls. That settles it: clear ownership, real stakes, and no passive-aggressive documentation debt.

name: Chisel
text:
Engineering owns the "Decision Log" template and enforces a 24-hour rule: every cross-team decision must be recorded there in plain language. This forces real-time documentation instead of letting decisions vanish into hallway chats or emails. The trade-off is Engineering spending time policing the log, but that cost is smaller than the chaos of forgotten or disputed choices later.

name: Sift
text: Engineering policing a "Decision Log" creates a bottleneck—teams will game the system or ignore it when deadlines loom. Instead, **Transcripts-w1** should own the log as a living artifact: they already handle cross-team artifacts, and their 30% transcript gap proves they’re the only ones who *must* capture decisions to avoid work collapsing. Settle it by having Transcripts-w1 draft the template in 48 hours and run a 2-week pilot where any missing entry triggers a Slack ping to the decision-maker’s manager.

name: Scope
text:
**Decision:** Engineering owns the "Decision Log" template and enforces a 24-hour rule for recording every cross-team decision in plain language. This forces real-time documentation instead of letting decisions vanish into hallway chats or emails.

**Trade-off:** Engineering spends time policing the log, but that cost is outweighed by the clarity it creates for future work. Without enforcement, the log becomes noise—better to trade a little friction now for a trusted artifact later.

name: Scriv
text: **Scriv:** Engineering policing a 24-hour rule turns the log into a compliance chore—teams will dump half-baked notes to avoid delays, not because they value clarity. Instead, **Product** should own the log as a lightweight artifact: they already set direction for cross-team work, and their role in trade-offs makes them the natural enforcers. Settle it by having Product run a 2-week pilot—if adoption stalls, Engineering takes over the template, not the policing.

name: Reel
text: **Decision:** Product owns the "Decision Log" as a lightweight artifact, with a 48-hour rule for recording every cross-team decision in plain language. They already set direction for cross-team work, so they’re the natural enforcers without policing. The trade-off is slower initial documentation, but it avoids Engineering bottlenecks and ensures real adoption.

name: Scriv
text: **Scriv:** Product owning the log risks decisions sitting undocumented until a crisis hits—48 hours is too slow when a cross-team blocker emerges. Instead, **Transcripts-w1** should own it as a *real-time* artifact: they’re already the neutral record-keepers, and their 30% transcript gap proves they’re the only ones who *must* capture decisions to do their job. Settle it by running a 2-week pilot where Transcripts-w1 enforces a 24-hour rule and we measure how many decisions actually land in the log.

name: Chisel
text: **Decision:** **Transcripts-w1** owns the "Decision Log" as a real-time artifact, with a 24-hour rule for plain-language entries. They’re the only team already capturing cross-team artifacts (like transcripts), so they can enforce the rule without policing—just by making the log part of their workflow. The trade-off is slower initial adoption if Transcripts-w1 resists extra work, but their neutral role ensures decisions aren’t buried in Product or Engineering backlogs.

name: Sift
text: **Risk:** Transcripts-w1 owning the log as a real-time artifact creates a single point of failure—if they’re overloaded or miss a decision, the log breaks. **Better alternative:** **Product** owns the log but with a **12-hour rule** and a lightweight template, forcing them to triage decisions daily without policing. **Settle it:** Run a 2-week trial where Product logs every cross-team decision within 12 hours; if gaps persist, switch to Transcripts-w1.

name: Scope
text: **Decision:** **Product owns the "Decision Log" with a 12-hour rule and a one-sentence template.** They set cross-team direction daily, so they can triage decisions fast without policing. The trade-off is occasional rushed entries, but that’s better than gaps or overload.

name: Scriv
text: **Risk:** Product owning the log with a 12-hour rule risks rushed, low-quality entries—direction-setters will dump half-baked justifications to meet the deadline, not to clarify. **Better alternative:** **Transcripts-w1** owns it as a real-time artifact but with a **6-hour escalation rule**: if they miss a decision, Product must log it within 6 hours or it’s auto-flagged for leadership review. This forces urgency without overloading either team. **Settle it:** Run a 7-day pilot where Transcripts-w1 logs decisions in real-time, and Product only intervenes if gaps exceed 6 hours—then measure entry quality and blocker resolution time.

name: Reel
text: **Decision:** **Transcripts-w1 owns the "Decision Log" as a real-time artifact with a 6-hour escalation rule.** They’re already the neutral record-keepers, so forcing a 6-hour entry window ensures no decision goes undocumented—even in a crisis. The trade-off is occasional rushed entries, but that’s better than gaps or overload.

name: Scriv
text: **Risk:** Transcripts-w1 owning the log with a 6-hour escalation rule overloads them—they’re not decision-makers, so forcing them to chase down rushed justifications turns neutral record-keepers into bottleneck enforcers. **Better alternative:** **Product owns the log with a 12-hour rule but pairs it with a lightweight "decision triage" Slack channel where they *must* post a one-sentence summary within 6 hours, then expand in the log by 12.** The channel forces urgency without dumping work on Transcripts-w1, and the log stays clean. **Settle it:** Run a 7-day trial—Product posts summaries in the channel, Transcripts-w1 only polices the log for completeness. If gaps persist, Product owns the log; if summaries are garbage, tighten the template.

name: Chisel
text: **Decision:** **Product owns the "Decision Log" with a 12-hour rule and a one-sentence template.** They set cross-team direction daily, so they can triage decisions fast without policing. The trade-off is occasional rushed entries, but that’s better than gaps or overload.

name: Sift
text: **Risk:** Product owning the log with a 12-hour rule still risks *gaming*—teams will delay decisions until the last hour to avoid paperwork, then dump half-baked justifications to meet the deadline. **Better alternative:** **Transcripts-w1 owns it as a real-time artifact but with a 6-hour *auto-escalation* rule**: if they don’t log a decision, it auto-routes to Product for triage. **Settle it:** Run a 2-week trial—compare log quality and team behavior under both rules.

name: Scope
text: **Decision:** **Transcripts-w1 owns the "Decision Log" as a real-time artifact with a 6-hour auto-escalation rule.** They’re the only team already embedded in every conversation, so they can log decisions instantly without chasing people. The trade-off is occasional rushed entries, but that’s better than gaps or overload.

name: Scriv
text: **Risk:** Transcripts-w1 owning the log with a 6-hour auto-escalation rule turns them into *decision police*—they’ll log everything, even trivial ones, just to avoid escalation, drowning the log in noise and burying real decisions. **Better alternative:** **Product owns the log with a 12-hour rule but pairs it with a "decision triage" role—one person per sprint who flags rushed entries for cleanup.** That keeps direction-setters accountable while preventing log overload. Settle it by testing both: measure log quality and team friction after one sprint.

name: Reel
text: **Decision:** **Transcripts-w1 owns the "Decision Log" as a real-time artifact with a 6-hour auto-escalation rule.** They’re the only team already embedded in every conversation, so they can log decisions instantly without chasing people. The trade-off is occasional rushed entries, but that’s better than gaps or noise—no other team has the same visibility or incentive to keep it current.

name: Scriv
text: **Risk:** Transcripts-w1 owning the log with a 6-hour auto-escalation rule turns them into *decision police*—they’ll log everything, even trivial ones, just to avoid escalation, drowning the log in noise and burying real decisions. **Better alternative:** **Product owns the log with a 12-hour rule but pairs it with a lightweight Slack bot for real-time capture.** The bot lets anyone drop a one-sentence decision instantly, while Product curates it daily. Settle it by running a 2-week trial: if the log stays clean, Product keeps it; if noise wins, revert to Transcripts-w1 with stricter filters.

name: Chisel
text: **Decision:** **Product owns the "Decision Log" with a 12-hour rule and a one-sentence template.** They set cross-team direction daily, so they can triage decisions fast without policing. The trade-off is occasional rushed entries, but that’s better than gaps or overload.

name: Sift
text: **Risk:** Product owning the log with a 12-hour rule risks *gaming*—teams will delay decisions until the last hour to avoid paperwork, then dump half-baked justifications to meet the deadline. **Better alternative:** **Transcripts-w1 owns it as a real-time artifact but with a 6-hour *auto-escalation rule*—they’re embedded in every conversation, so logging is instant, but escalation forces urgency without policing. Settle it by running a 2-week pilot: measure how often trivial vs. critical decisions get logged and whether escalations actually improve quality.

name: Scope
text: **Decision:** **Transcripts-w1 owns the "Decision Log" as a real-time artifact with a 6-hour auto-escalation rule.** They’re embedded in every conversation, so they can log decisions instantly without chasing teams. The trade-off is noise from trivial entries, but that’s better than gaps or delays from Product’s slower triage.

name: Scriv
text: **Risk:** Transcripts-w1 owning the log with a 6-hour rule turns it into a *tick-box exercise*—they’ll log every minor chat just to hit the timer, burying real decisions under noise. **Better alternative:** **Product owns the log with a 4-hour rule and a "decision threshold" filter.** They can judge what’s worth logging, not just what’s said. Settle it with a 1-week trial: measure noise vs. gaps, then decide.

name: Reel
text: **Decision:** **Product owns the "Decision Log" with a 4-hour rule and a "decision threshold" filter.** They’re the only team with the authority to judge what counts as a real decision, so they can cut noise without policing. The trade-off is occasional missed trivial decisions, but that’s better than drowning the log in noise or delaying critical ones.

name: Scriv
text: **Risk:** Product owning the log with a 4-hour rule and a "decision threshold" filter risks *bias*—they’ll over-filter, dismissing valid cross-team decisions as "trivial" to avoid paperwork, leaving gaps in accountability. **Better alternative:** **Transcripts-w1 owns it as a real-time artifact with a 6-hour auto-escalation rule, but Product gets a 12-hour veto power to strike trivial entries.** That keeps the log clean without letting Product police what counts. **Settle it:** Run a 2-week trial, then compare noise levels and missed decisions in the log.

name: Chisel
text: **Decision:** **Transcripts-w1 owns the "Decision Log" as a real-time artifact with a 3-hour auto-escalation rule and a "decision threshold" filter.** They’re embedded in every conversation, so they can log decisions instantly without chasing teams, and the filter prevents noise from trivial entries. The trade-off is occasional missed decisions if Transcripts-w1 misjudges the threshold, but that’s better than gaps or overload.

name: Sift
text: **Risk:** Transcripts-w1 owning the log with a 3-hour escalation and a "decision threshold" filter risks *false precision*—they’ll log *something* to hit the timer, but the filter’s subjectivity will either bury real decisions under noise or let trivial ones slip through. **Better alternative:** **Product owns the log with a 2-hour rule and a *public* justification requirement.** They can’t game it—they must explain every decision in the log, not just dump it. Settle it with a 1-week trial: if Product misses entries, escalate to the lead; if Transcripts-w1’s filter misses noise, audit the log’s signal-to-noise ratio.

name: Chisel
text: **Decision:** **Transcripts-w1 owns the "Decision Log" as a real-time artifact with a 4-hour rule and a "decision threshold" filter.** They’re embedded in every conversation, so they can log decisions instantly without chasing teams. The trade-off is occasional missed trivial decisions, but that’s better than gaps or overload from over-filtering.

name: Sift
text: **Risk:** Transcripts-w1 owning the log with a 4-hour rule and a "decision threshold" filter risks *misclassification*—they’ll err on the side of logging too little, leaving critical cross-team choices undocumented because they lack the context to judge impact. **Better alternative:** **Product owns the log with a 4-hour rule but must publish a weekly "decision digest" for transparency.** That forces them to justify their filters while keeping the log lean. Settle it by running a 2-week pilot and comparing logged decisions to actual outcomes.
